subject: Hosted API pricing + overage / spend cap options
messages:

Subject: Hosted API rate card + what happens if we exceed our monthly budget

Hi Marissa,

Thanks for the demo last week — the latency numbers look great. Procurement asked me to get a formal rate card and clarification on how Redwood handles overages. Two specific questions: 

1) Can you share the hosted API baseline rates (tokens per $ / embedding unit cost) and any volume break pricing?
2) If we accidentally exceed our committed or expected monthly spend, what mechanisms does Redwood provide to prevent surprise charges? For example, can you enforce a hard spend cap, or do you rely on alerts and manual intervention?

We prefer an arrangement where we aren’t unexpectedly charged more than our forecast without explicit approval. If a hard cut is not available for hosted API, what guardrails do you recommend?

I can loop in our procurement team if you want to coordinate paperwork.

—Jordan
Jordan Hayes
Director, AI Products
Acme Analytics
[jordan.hayes@acme-analytics.com]
From: Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.com>

Cc: Rishi Malhotra <rishi_malhotra@redwood.com>
Date: Tue, 10 Feb 2026 11:03:00 -0500
Subject: Re: Hosted API rate card + what happens if we exceed our monthly budget

Hi Jordan — thanks for the clear questions. Attaching our current hosted rate card and a short mutual action plan for next steps. [attachment: redwood-rate-card.pdf (PDF), mutual-action-plan.xlsx (XLSX)]

Quick answers up front: 
- Baseline hosted rates: see attached PDF. Short summary: text generation is $0.0025 / 1K tokens at baseline; embeddings are $0.005 / 1K vectors (these are example rates; final pricing can include volume tiers).
- Overage handling (hosted API): we provide three guardrails you can use in combination:
  1) Billing alerts (recommended): configurable thresholds (e.g., 50%, 75%, 90%) with email/Slack notifications.
  2) Soft spend cap (default): account-level throttle when you hit the monthly cap that will start returning 429s for new requests unless an override is approved. This prevents additional usage but can degrade UX — good for non-critical workflows.
  3) Hard cutoff (by exception): for hosted customers we can enable an enforced billing lock that blocks all further requests once the cap is hit. This requires a signed amendment and acceptance of potential downtime; we only enable it for customers who explicitly request it.

Other options: move to Redwood Dedicated (reserved capacity) or a pre-paid commitment which gives predictable spend and avoids overage surprises.

If you want, Rishi and I can sketch the exact wording for the MSA amendment to enable a hard cutoff and the SLA caveats.

Next steps: if you confirm the threshold and whether you prefer soft vs hard handling, we’ll add it to the mutual action plan and share an updated DocuSign link.

Best,
Marissa Cole
Senior Solutions Engineer | Redwood Inference
marissa_cole@redwood.com
From: Rishi Malhotra <rishi_malhotra@redwood.com>
To: Jordan Hayes <jordan.hayes@acme-analytics.com>, Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.com>
Date: Wed, 11 Feb 2026 08:27:00 -0500
Subject: Re: Hosted API rate card + what happens if we exceed our monthly budget

Jordan — quick note from pricing side: we can offer two pragmatic approaches that customers commonly choose: 

A) Guardrails + Alerts (low friction): set a soft cap at 110% of forecast + 90/95% alerts. We’ll automatically throttle at 100% and notify you; your engineering team can request an emergency override if needed. For this we don’t change the MSA.

B) Commitment + Hard Cap (procurement-friendly): if Acme signs a small monthly commitment (e.g., $25k/mo) we’ll: 1) give a baseline 10% volume discount, and 2) optionally enable a hard billing lock that blocks further usage after the committed amount is exhausted. Enabling the hard lock requires an amendment to the hosted terms (we document the exact failure mode — 403 errors with a clear billing-exceeded code) and acceptance of the operational impact.

We typically avoid enabling hard locks without commitments because it creates a high support lift when customers expect continued service. Happy to draft both options in clear contract language.

—Rishi
Director, Commercial Pricing | Redwood Inference
From: Procurement Team <procurement@acme-analytics.com>
To: Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.com>, Rishi Malhotra <rishi_malhotra@redwood.com>
Date: Thu, 12 Feb 2026 14:10:00 -0500
Subject: Re: Hosted API rate card + what happens if we exceed our monthly budget

Thanks — this is helpful. A couple follow-ups from Procurement: 
1) If we take option B (commitment + hard cap), will Redwood give us an exception window (e.g., a one-time emergency override) without requiring full MS amendment each time? We want a documented, auditable process for overrides.
2) For option A, how quickly do throttled requests fail and how are they surfaced to our SREs (error codes, headers)? We need to be sure our pipelines can detect and retry or fallback safely.

Also please send the DocuSign for the MSA + the amendment language for the hard lock so our legal team can review.

—Procurement (on behalf of Jordan)
From: Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.com>
To: Procurement Team <procurement@acme-analytics.com>, Jordan Hayes <jordan.hayes@acme-analytics.com>
Cc: Rishi Malhotra <rishi_malhotra@redwood.com>, Sergio Alvarez <sergio_alvarez@redwood.com>
Date: Mon, 16 Feb 2026 15:28:00 -0500
Subject: Re: Hosted API rate card + what happens if we exceed our monthly budget

Hi — quick answers and next steps below.

1) Override workflow (for option B): we can include an "emergency override" clause in the amendment: a documented, one-time manual override request that must be initiated by an approved Acme admin and confirmed by Redwood Sales Ops. Overrides are logged, time-limited (e.g., 4 hours), and require email confirmation to be auditable. We will add that exact language to the amendment.

2) Throttle failure mode (for option A): when the soft cap is hit the API returns HTTP 429 with JSON body including "error_code": "usage_cap_reached" and a header X-Redwood-Cap-Remaining: 0. Retries within 5 minutes will continue to receive 429 unless usage drops or you request an override. We recommend exponential backoff + a secondary fallback model or cache serving for critical paths.

3) Operational recommendation: set alerts at 75% and 90%, but configure the soft cap at 110% of your forecast to avoid immediate disruption from small bursts. If Acme needs strict zero-overage billing, option B + hard lock is the correct path.

4) Paperwork: Rishi and I will draft the amendment and update the mutual action plan. I’ll send the DocuSign link once we have the amendment text.

Attached: redwood-rate-card.pdf (attached earlier), mutual-action-plan.xlsx (updated row: spend-cap preference).

If you can confirm which option (A or B) Acme prefers, we’ll prioritize the amendment or the ops playbook.

Thanks,
Marissa
Senior Solutions Engineer | Redwood Inference
